submodules.title: 1. Why Smart People Make Money Mistakes
submodules.intro: If we know what to do, why do we often do the opposite?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHY SMART PEOPLE MAKE MONEY MISTAKES
Behavioural finance studies how feelings and mental shortcuts push people away from sensible money choices. It does not say people are foolish. It says that every human brain, including yours, has habits that can hurt an investor. Knowing them is the first defence. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Try this puzzle fast: a bat and a ball cost ₹110 together, and the bat costs ₹100 more than the ball. Most people blurt out that the ball costs ₹10, but the answer is ₹5.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TWO WAYS OF THINKING
• Fast thinking: quick, automatic and emotional. It is great for catching a ball and poor for investing decisions.
• Slow thinking: careful, effortful and logical. It is the one you need when money is involved.
• Mistakes happen when fast thinking answers a question that needs slow thinking.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHERE MONEY MISTAKES COME FROM
• Emotions: fear makes people sell low and greed makes them buy high.
• Mental shortcuts: rules of thumb that are usually fine but sometimes badly wrong.
• Social pressure: copying friends, family and social media.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT
• Name the bias when you notice it. Naming it slows you down.
• Write rules in advance, while you are calm.
• Keep a journal so you can see your own patterns.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE PANIC SELL
Aarav's fictional simulator portfolio of ₹1,00,000 drops 10% to ₹90,000 after a scary headline. He feels sick and sells everything. Over the next three months, in this made-up example, it recovers to ₹1,05,000. If he had stayed invested, he would have ₹1,05,000, so his panic cost him 1,05,000 - 90,000 = ₹15,000 compared with holding. Meera says the market did not hurt him. His fast thinking did.

🧪 TRY IT: CATCH THE TRICK
Solve the puzzle slowly: a bat and a ball cost ₹110 together, and the bat costs ₹100 more than the ball. What does the ball cost?
(Answer: if the ball is ₹5, the bat is ₹105 and together they cost ₹110, with the bat ₹100 more. The ball costs ₹5, not ₹10. Slow thinking catches what fast thinking misses.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Everyone has mental shortcuts and emotions that can hurt their money choices. Notice them, slow down and write your rules in advance.

quiz.question: What does behavioural finance study?
options: How feelings and mental shortcuts affect money choices
quiz.explanation: It looks at the human side of money decisions.

quiz.question: A bat and a ball cost ₹110 and the bat costs ₹100 more than the ball. What is the ball's price?
quiz.explanation: Ball ₹5 plus bat ₹105 gives ₹110, and the bat is ₹100 more.

quiz.question: Which kind of thinking is best for big money decisions?
quiz.explanation: Slow thinking checks facts and avoids snap reactions.

quiz.question: What does fear tend to make investors do?
quiz.explanation: Fear often leads to selling after a drop.

quiz.question: What is a good first defence against a bias?
options: Name it and write rules in advance
quiz.explanation: Spotting the bias and having a rule gives you time to think.

submodules.title: 2. Loss Aversion and Prospect Theory
submodules.intro: Why does losing ₹1,000 hurt more than gaining ₹1,000 feels good?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: LOSS AVERSION AND PROSPECT THEORY
Research by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, who introduced prospect theory in 1979, found that people feel losses more strongly than equal gains. This is called loss aversion. It explains why people hold losing shares for too long and sell winners too fast. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
In many studies, a loss feels roughly twice as strong as a gain of the same size, though the exact figure varies from person to person.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE CORE IDEAS
• Loss aversion: a loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases.
• Reference point: people judge results against a starting point, such as their purchase price, not against the final amount.
• Risk mood flips: people tend to avoid risk when they can win and to take risk when they face a sure loss.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: EXPECTED VALUE
• Expected value = chance of each outcome x its amount, added up.
• A 50% chance of ₹10,000 has an expected value of 0.5 x 10,000 = ₹5,000.
• Two choices can have the same expected value and still feel very different.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW IT HURTS INVESTORS
• Refusing to sell a loser because selling makes the loss real.
• Selling a winner quickly to lock in the happy feeling.
• Checking a portfolio often, which shows more red days and more pain.

🍕 MINI CASE: SURE THING OR GAMBLE
In a classroom game, Meera can take a sure ₹5,000 or a coin flip: 50% chance of ₹10,000 and 50% chance of nothing. The expected value of the flip is 0.5 x 10,000 = ₹5,000, the same as the sure amount. Most students take the sure ₹5,000. Now the game flips: a sure loss of ₹5,000 or a coin flip with a 50% chance of losing ₹10,000 and a 50% chance of losing nothing. Many students now choose the gamble, because a sure loss hurts so much.

🧪 TRY IT: WORK OUT THE VALUE
A fictional game offers a 25% chance of winning ₹8,000 and a 75% chance of winning nothing. What is the expected value? Would a sure ₹2,500 be better, equal or worse in pure expected value?
(Answer: expected value = 0.25 x 8,000 = ₹2,000. A sure ₹2,500 is higher, so it is better in expected value.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Losses feel stronger than gains, which pushes people to hold losers and sell winners. Judging choices by expected value, not by feeling, helps.

quiz.question: What is loss aversion?
options: Losses feeling stronger than equal gains
quiz.explanation: A loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases.

quiz.question: Who introduced prospect theory?
quiz.explanation: Kahneman and Tversky introduced it in 1979.

quiz.question: What is the expected value of a 50% chance of winning ₹10,000?
A 25% chance of ₹8,000 has what expected value?
How does loss aversion often hurt investors?
options: They hold losing shares too long to avoid making the loss real
quiz.explanation: Selling a loser makes the loss real, so people delay.

submodules.title: 3. Overconfidence and the Illusion of Control
submodules.intro: Why do most people think they are better than average?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: OVERCONFIDENCE AND THE ILLUSION OF CONTROL
Overconfidence is believing you know more, or can predict better, than you really can. A few lucky wins can make a beginner feel like an expert. This leads to bigger bets, more trades and higher costs. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
In some surveys, most people rate themselves as above-average drivers, which cannot be true for everyone.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: SIGNS OF OVERCONFIDENCE
• Trading very often.
• Putting too much money into one idea because you are 'sure'.
• Crediting skill for wins and bad luck for losses.
• Believing you can time the market.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: ILLUSION OF CONTROL
• Feeling that more research, more screens or more checking gives control over a random outcome.
• Short-term price moves have a large random part that no one controls.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE COST OF TOO MANY TRADES
• Every trade costs brokerage, taxes and the gap between buy and sell prices.
• Yearly cost % = (trades per year x cost per trade) ÷ portfolio value x 100.
• Studies of individual investors often find that those who trade the most earn less.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO TRADING STYLES
Aarav makes 20 trades a month in his fictional ₹1,00,000 account at ₹60 each. That is 20 x 60 = ₹1,200 a month, or ₹14,400 a year, which is 14.4% of the account in costs alone. Meera makes 2 trades a month, which is 2 x 60 x 12 = ₹1,440 a year, or 1.44%. Aarav needs a 14.4% gain just to break even. Meera keeps a journal and notes when she wins by luck.

🧪 TRY IT: COUNT THE COSTS
A fictional trader makes 10 trades a month at ₹50 each in a ₹50,000 account. What is the yearly cost in rupees and as a percentage of the account?
(Answer: 10 x 50 x 12 = ₹6,000 a year, which is 6,000 ÷ 50,000 x 100 = 12% of the account.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Overconfidence leads to bigger bets and more trades, and trading costs add up. Treat wins with humility and keep records.

quiz.question: What is overconfidence?
options: Believing you know more or can predict better than you really can
quiz.explanation: It means overrating your own knowledge or skill.

quiz.question: What is the illusion of control?
options: Feeling you control an outcome that is largely random
quiz.explanation: More screens do not control random moves.

quiz.question: 20 trades a month at ₹60 each cost how much per year?
What is 10 trades a month at ₹50 each in a ₹50,000 account, as a yearly cost percentage?
What is a good habit after a win?
options: Note whether luck helped and record the reason
quiz.explanation: Honest records separate skill from luck.

submodules.title: 4. Herd Behaviour and FOMO
submodules.intro: Why does everyone seem to buy at the very same time?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: HERD BEHAVIOUR AND FOMO
Humans copy each other, which is useful in daily life and risky in markets. Herd behaviour is following the crowd without checking the facts. FOMO, the fear of missing out, is the pain of watching others make money. Both push people to buy after a big rise, when prices are already high. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Prices that rise on social media excitement can turn around fast once the crowd runs out of new buyers.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW THE HERD WORKS
• Rising prices attract attention, attention attracts buyers and buyers lift prices further.
• Friends and online posts make a trade feel safe because many people are doing it.
• When the crowd turns, everyone tries to leave at once.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: FOMO WARNING SIGNS
• You want to buy only because the price is already up a lot.
• You cannot explain what the business does.
• You feel rushed and fear that the chance will vanish.
• The idea came from a stranger's post or a group chat.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO DO INSTEAD
• Pause for at least a day.
• Check the facts: business, valuation, risk and your plan.
• Ask: would I want this share if nobody else were talking about it?
• Remember that there will always be another opportunity.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE LATE BUYER
A fictional share, RocketTech, rises five days in a row, from ₹100 to ₹140. Friends brag in a chat group and Aarav buys at ₹140. Soon it falls back to ₹112, a loss of 140 - 112 = ₹28, which is 28 ÷ 140 = 20%. Meera, who checked the facts and found no news behind the jump, stayed out.

🧪 TRY IT: EARLY VERSUS LATE
A fictional share rises from ₹200 to ₹320 and then falls 25%. What is the price after the fall? How much does a buyer at ₹320 lose, and what is the result for a buyer at ₹200?
(Answer: the fall is 25% of 320 = 80, so the price is ₹240. The ₹320 buyer loses 80 ÷ 320 x 100 = 25%. The ₹200 buyer is still up (240 - 200) ÷ 200 x 100 = 20%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Following the crowd after a big rise often means buying high. Pause, check the facts and stick to your plan.

quiz.question: What is herd behaviour?
options: Following the crowd without checking facts
quiz.explanation: It means copying others without your own analysis.

quiz.question: What does FOMO stand for?
quiz.explanation: FOMO is the fear of missing out.

quiz.question: A share bought at ₹140 falls to ₹112. What is the loss percentage?
Which is a FOMO warning sign?
options: You want to buy mainly because the price is already up a lot
quiz.explanation: Chasing a price rise is a classic FOMO sign.

quiz.question: What is a good response to a hot tip from a group chat?
options: Pause and check the facts before acting
quiz.explanation: A pause and fact check protects you from herd moves.

submodules.title: 5. Anchoring and Confirmation Bias
submodules.intro: Why do we cling to one number and ignore facts we dislike?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: ANCHORING AND CONFIRMATION BIAS
Anchoring means your mind sticks to the first number you saw, such as the price you paid or a share's old high. Confirmation bias means you notice facts that agree with you and ignore facts that do not. Together they can trap you in a bad position. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Studies show that even a random number, like one from a spin of a wheel, can pull people's guesses toward it.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: ANCHORING
• Your purchase price is an anchor, but the market does not know or care what you paid.
• A share's 52-week high feels like where it 'should' trade.
• Ask: would I buy this today at today's price?

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CONFIRMATION BIAS
• You read only positive news about a share you own.
• You follow people who agree with you and mute those who disagree.
• A strong idea should survive the best arguments against it.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE BREAKEVEN TRAP
• Gain needed to break even = (purchase price - current price) ÷ current price x 100.
• Waiting to 'get back to even' may mean missing better uses of the money.

🍕 MINI CASE: WAITING TO GET EVEN
Aarav bought a fictional share at ₹500 and it is now ₹400. He says he will sell only when it returns to ₹500. The gain needed is (500 - 400) ÷ 400 x 100 = 25%. Meera asks him a different question: if he had ₹400 in cash today, would he buy this share? If the answer is no, the ₹500 anchor is the only reason he is holding.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE CLIMB
A fictional share was bought at ₹300 and is now ₹225. What gain is needed to get back to ₹300?
(Answer: (300 - 225) ÷ 225 x 100 = 75 ÷ 225 x 100 = 33.3%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Your purchase price is only a memory, not a reason. Ask whether you would buy at today's price, and seek out views that disagree with you.

quiz.question: What is anchoring?
options: Sticking to the first number you saw
quiz.explanation: The mind clings to an early number such as a purchase price.

quiz.question: What is confirmation bias?
options: Noticing facts that agree with you and ignoring the rest
quiz.explanation: It means favouring information that supports your view.

quiz.question: A share bought at ₹500 is now ₹400. What gain brings it back to ₹500?
Which question helps break the anchoring trap?
options: What was the high last year?
Would I buy this today at today's price?
quiz.explanation: It ignores the old price and judges today's facts.

quiz.question: What is a good response to confirmation bias?
options: Seek the best arguments against your idea
quiz.explanation: Strong ideas survive opposing arguments.

submodules.title: 6. The Disposition Effect and Sunk Costs
submodules.intro: Why do people sell winners too soon and keep losers too long?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE DISPOSITION EFFECT AND SUNK COSTS
The disposition effect is the habit of selling winning shares early to lock in a gain and holding losing shares to avoid a loss. It was described by Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman in 1985. A related trap is the sunk cost fallacy: continuing something because of money already spent. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A winning share can feel like a trophy to cash in, and a losing share can feel like an unfinished fight, even though the market treats both the same.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE PATTERN
• Winners are sold early because gains feel fragile.
• Losers are kept because selling makes the loss real.
• Over time, this cuts good ideas short and lets bad ideas run.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: SUNK COSTS
• A sunk cost is money already spent that you cannot get back.
• It should not decide your next move. Only the future outlook should.
• Ask: knowing what I know now, would I start this again today?

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: A BETTER APPROACH
• Decide sell rules before you buy: a stop-loss and a target or a reason to exit.
• Judge each holding on its future, not on how you feel about its past.
• Review winners and losers on the same rules.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO SHARES, TWO MISTAKES
Meera's fictional simulator holds two shares worth ₹10,000 each. Share A rises 20% to ₹12,000 and Aarav would sell it for a quick win. Share B falls 20% to ₹8,000 and he would hold on to avoid the loss. Later A reaches ₹15,000 and B falls to ₹6,000. By selling A early, he banked ₹2,000 instead of ₹5,000, missing ₹3,000. By holding B, the loss grew from ₹2,000 to ₹4,000.

🧪 TRY IT: ASK THE FRESH QUESTION
A fictional share was bought at ₹100 and is now ₹70, with weak business news. You have ₹7,000 in it. If you had ₹7,000 in cash today, would you buy it? What does the ₹30 per share loss have to do with the decision?
(Answer: if you would not buy it today, the case for holding is weak. The ₹30 loss is a sunk cost and should not decide the next step, only the future outlook should.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long hurts results. Set exit rules in advance and judge holdings on their future, not their past.

quiz.question: What is the disposition effect?
options: Selling winners early and holding losers too long
quiz.explanation: It is the pattern of locking in gains and avoiding losses.

quiz.question: What is a sunk cost?
options: A cost you can still avoid
Money already spent that cannot be recovered
quiz.explanation: A sunk cost is gone and should not drive future choices.

quiz.question: Two shares of ₹10,000 each: A rises 20% and B falls 20%. What are their values?
Which question helps beat the sunk cost trap?
options: What did I pay for it?
Would I start this position again today?
quiz.explanation: It focuses on the future, not on past spending.

quiz.question: When is the best time to decide on a stop-loss?
quiz.explanation: Rules made in advance are calmer and clearer.

submodules.title: 7. Mental Accounting and 'House Money'
submodules.intro: Is a rupee from a gift different from a rupee you earned?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: MENTAL ACCOUNTING AND HOUSE MONEY
Mental accounting is the habit of treating money differently depending on where it came from or what it is for, even though a rupee is a rupee. Economist Richard Thaler described the idea. It can lead to unwise choices, like taking big risks with 'free' money. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
People often spend a surprise bonus or a gift more freely than the same amount earned through hard work, though the money is identical.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON MENTAL ACCOUNTS
• Salary money feels serious. Gift money feels free.
• Profits from the market feel like 'house money', which people risk more easily.
• Savings and spending money are kept in separate mental boxes.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHERE IT GOES WRONG
• Risking profits recklessly because they feel like a bonus.
• Keeping low-interest savings while paying high-interest debt.
• Treating a tax refund or prize as spare cash while ignoring bigger goals.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHEN IT HELPS
• Separate accounts for goals, such as an emergency fund, can be useful discipline.
• The key is to follow rules on purpose, not by accident, and to remember that all money is the same money.

🍕 MINI CASE: SAME MONEY, TWO HANDS
In a school quiz, Aarav wins ₹5,000 in his fictional simulator story and treats it as free money, so he puts all of it into one risky idea. Meera treats her ₹5,000 prize like any other money and follows her usual position limit. Another example: a fictional family keeps ₹20,000 in savings at 3% while owing ₹20,000 on a loan at 12%. The loan costs 20,000 x 0.12 = ₹2,400 a year and the savings earn 20,000 x 0.03 = ₹600, a net loss of ₹1,800 a year.

🧪 TRY IT: SPOT THE LEAK
A fictional family holds ₹50,000 in savings earning 4% a year while owing ₹50,000 on a loan at 10%. What is the yearly interest paid, the yearly interest earned and the net difference?
(Answer: interest paid = 50,000 x 0.10 = ₹5,000. Interest earned = 50,000 x 0.04 = ₹2,000. Net cost = ₹3,000 a year, which a family should discuss with a trusted adult.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A rupee is a rupee wherever it came from. Treat all money by the same rules and watch for mental boxes that hide bad trade-offs.

quiz.question: What is mental accounting?
options: Treating money differently depending on its source or label
quiz.explanation: Mental accounting treats equal money unequally.

quiz.question: What does 'house money' mean in this lesson?
options: Profits that feel free and so are risked more easily
quiz.explanation: People risk winnings more freely than their own money.

quiz.question: ₹20,000 at 12% interest costs how much per year?
Savings earn 3% and a loan costs 12% on the same ₹20,000. What is the yearly net loss?
What is a sensible approach to prize or bonus money?
options: Treat it by the same rules as other money
quiz.explanation: A rupee is a rupee, so the same rules apply.

submodules.title: 8. Recency, Hindsight and the Gambler's Fallacy
submodules.intro: Why do we expect recent patterns to continue, or to reverse?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: RECENCY, HINDSIGHT AND THE GAMBLER'S FALLACY
Our minds love patterns, even in randomness. Recency bias gives too much weight to what just happened. Hindsight bias makes past events feel obvious, as though we knew them all along. The gambler's fallacy is the belief that a streak must reverse. All three can mislead an investor. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
After a fair coin lands heads five times, the chance of heads on the next flip is still exactly 50%.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RECENCY BIAS
• After a strong year, many people expect more of the same.
• After a crash, they expect more crashes.
• Long-term averages matter more than the latest few weeks.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HINDSIGHT BIAS
• After an event, it feels like it was predictable. 'I knew it!'
• This makes people overrate their skill and learn the wrong lessons.
• A written prediction made beforehand is the cure.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: STREAKS AND PROBABILITY
• Chance of a given result in a row = (chance each time) multiplied together.
• Five heads in a row has a chance of (1/2) x (1/2) x (1/2) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/32, about 3.1%, but the next flip is still 50-50.
• A winning streak in the market does not prove skill, and a losing streak does not mean a win is due.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE STREAK
The fictional Sundar Foods Ltd rises five days in a row, and Aarav assumes a sixth rise is certain. Meera reminds him that five heads in a row from a fair coin happens about once in 32 tries, and yet the next flip is still 50%. She writes her own prediction in her journal before each week, so she can later check it honestly without hindsight.

🧪 TRY IT: COIN CHECK
What is the chance of three heads in a row from a fair coin? After three heads, what is the chance that the fourth flip is heads?
(Answer: (1/2) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/8 = 12.5%. The fourth flip is still 50%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Streaks and recent events feel meaningful, but randomness has no memory. Record predictions before the outcome to defeat hindsight.

quiz.question: What is recency bias?
options: Giving too much weight to recent events
quiz.explanation: It overweights what just happened.

quiz.question: What is hindsight bias?
options: Past events feeling obvious after they happen
quiz.explanation: Afterwards, events seem to have been predictable.

quiz.question: After 5 heads in a row, what is the chance of heads on the next flip of a fair coin?
quiz.explanation: A fair coin has no memory.

quiz.question: What is the chance of 3 heads in a row from a fair coin?
What helps defeat hindsight bias?
options: Written predictions made before the outcome
quiz.explanation: A written record shows what you really thought.

submodules.title: 9. Bubbles, Panics and Market Cycles
submodules.intro: Why do prices swing far beyond what a business is worth?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: BUBBLES, PANICS AND MARKET CYCLES
A bubble happens when prices rise far above what the underlying value can support, driven by excitement and the hope of selling to someone else at a higher price. A panic is the opposite, with prices falling beyond reason. Studying them helps you spot the same emotions in yourself. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
In 1630s Holland, prices of tulip bulbs soared and then collapsed. Historians still debate how extreme it really was, but the story remains a classic warning.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE EMOTION CYCLE
• Optimism, excitement and euphoria come as prices rise. Euphoria often marks the top.
• Anxiety, fear, panic and despair come as prices fall. Despair often marks the bottom.
• Hope returns, and the cycle begins again.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: SIGNS OF A BUBBLE
• Prices far above what earnings or assets can justify.
• Stories like 'this time is different'.
• New investors rushing in, borrowing to buy, and everyone talking about it.
• A valuation measure like P/E far above its usual range.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: STAYING SANE
• Keep a long-term plan and a diversified mix.
• Compare the price with the value of the business.
• Be careful when everyone is euphoric and curious when everyone is fearful.

🍕 MINI CASE: WHEN THE STORY RUNS AHEAD
A fictional share earns ₹10 per share and trades at ₹200, a P/E of 20. During a frenzy the price reaches ₹800 while earnings only grow to ₹11, so P/E is about 800 ÷ 11 = 72.7. When excitement fades and P/E returns to 20, the price is 20 x 11 = ₹220. From ₹800 that is a fall of (800 - 220) ÷ 800 = 72.5%. The business did fine. The price had simply run far ahead.

🧪 TRY IT: WHAT IF P/E RETURNS
A fictional share trades at ₹600 with earnings of ₹12 per share, so P/E is 50. If P/E falls back to 25 and earnings stay at ₹12, what is the price and the percentage fall?
(Answer: price = 25 x 12 = ₹300. The fall is (600 - 300) ÷ 600 x 100 = 50%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Bubbles and panics are driven by emotion, not value. Watch the price against the business and keep a plan for both the excitement and the fear.

quiz.question: What is a bubble?
options: Prices rising far above what value supports
quiz.explanation: Bubbles are prices detached from underlying value.

quiz.question: Which emotion often marks the top of a market cycle?
quiz.explanation: Euphoria is common near peaks.

quiz.question: A share trades at ₹600 with earnings of ₹12. What is the P/E?
If that P/E falls to 25 with earnings unchanged, what is the price?
Which phrase is a common warning sign of a bubble?
quiz.explanation: 'This time is different' appears in many bubbles.

submodules.title: 10. Finfluencers, Tips and Scams
submodules.intro: How do you protect yourself from bad advice and fraud?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: FINFLUENCERS, TIPS AND SCAMS
Social media, group chats and videos are full of money advice. Some of it is good education, and some of it is hype or fraud. In India, giving paid investment advice generally needs registration with SEBI, and the regulator has acted against unregistered advisers and misleading 'finfluencers'. Learn to check before you trust. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A promise of 10% returns every week sounds small, but over a year it would turn ₹1,00,000 into about 142 times that amount. No real investment can do this.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RED FLAGS
• Guaranteed or very high returns with no risk.
• Pressure to act now before a 'chance' disappears.
• Secret tips sold in private groups.
• Asking you to send money to a personal account, or to share passwords or OTPs.
• Advisers who show only winning trades.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON SCHEMES
• Pump and dump: promoters hype a tiny share, prices jump, they sell, and the price collapses on later buyers.
• Ponzi scheme: early investors are paid with new investors' money until it collapses.
• Fake apps and fake trading groups that copy real brands.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW TO CHECK
• Ask whether the person is a SEBI-registered adviser or analyst, and check SEBI's official list.
• Search for the same claim on trusted sources.
• Never share OTPs, passwords or card details.
• Show tips to a parent, teacher or guardian before acting.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE PUMP AND DUMP
A fictional tiny share trades at ₹10. A chat group hypes it and the price jumps to ₹30, a rise of 200%. The organisers sell at the top and the price collapses to ₹8. Aarav bought at ₹30, so his loss is 30 - 8 = ₹22 per share, which is 22 ÷ 30 = 73.3%. Meera noticed that nobody could explain the business and stayed away.

🧪 TRY IT: CHECK THE PROMISE
A fictional group promises 5% growth every week. Is that believable? Think about what 5% a week would mean over a year, and what the group should show you before you trust it.
(Answer: 5% a week compounds to about 1.05 to the power of 52, which is roughly 12.6 times your money in a year, far beyond what any real investment reliably gives. A trustworthy adviser should show SEBI registration and explain the risks. Never send money to a stranger.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Hype and guaranteed returns are red flags. Check registration, never share OTPs and passwords, and show tips to a trusted adult first.

submodules.title: 11. Habits and Rules That Beat Emotions
submodules.intro: How can you set things up so good decisions happen almost automatically?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: HABITS AND RULES THAT BEAT EMOTIONS
You cannot switch off your emotions, but you can build rules and habits so that emotions have less power. The idea is precommitment: deciding in advance, when you are calm, what you will do later, when you are not. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Ulysses in the old Greek story had his sailors tie him to the mast so he could hear the sirens' song without steering the ship onto the rocks. A good rule works like the rope.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RULES TO WRITE DOWN
• The most I will risk on one idea, such as 1% of capital.
• The most I will put in one share, such as 10% of the portfolio.
• When I will sell, written before I buy.
• A waiting period, such as 24 hours, before any new idea.
• When I will review and rebalance.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HABITS THAT HELP
• Automate: a SIP invests on a schedule without a daily decision.
• Check your portfolio less often. More checks show more red days and more pain.
• Mute hype accounts and limit how much market news you read.
• Keep a journal with a column for your feelings.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHEN YOU WANT TO BREAK A RULE
• Write down why, wait a day and ask a parent, teacher or guardian.
• If the reason is a feeling like fear or excitement, the rule is doing its job.
• Update rules only during a calm review, not in the middle of a trade.

🍕 MINI CASE: MEERA'S RULEBOOK
Meera's fictional simulator account has ₹1,00,000. Her rules: risk no more than 1%, which is ₹1,000 per idea, hold no more than 10% in a single share, which is ₹10,000, write the stop-loss before buying and wait 24 hours before any new idea. She also sets a SIP of ₹2,000 a month, which invests ₹24,000 over 12 months with no daily decisions. When a shiny tip arrives, her rules tell her what to do.

🧪 TRY IT: WRITE YOUR RULES
Write three rules for a simulator account of ₹50,000. How much is 1% risk per idea, and how much is a 10% position cap?
(Answer: 1% of 50,000 = ₹500 and 10% of 50,000 = ₹5,000. Example rules: risk at most ₹500 per idea, hold at most ₹5,000 in one share, and wait 24 hours before buying.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Rules and habits written in calm moments protect you in emotional ones. Automate, wait, and review on a schedule.

quiz.question: What is precommitment?
options: Deciding in advance, while calm, what you will do later
quiz.explanation: Precommitment sets the rule before emotions arrive.

quiz.explanation: Frequent checks expose you to more noise and fear.

When should you change your rules?

quiz.explanation: Calm reviews protect the rules from emotional edits.

submodules.title: 12. Your Behaviour Journal and Mind Checklist
submodules.intro: How do you turn all these ideas into a routine that keeps you honest?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE MIND CHECKLIST
You now know the main traps: panic, loss aversion, overconfidence, the herd, anchors, sunk costs, mental boxes, streaks, bubbles and scams. This capstone puts them into a checklist and a journal for your simulator practice. The goal is self-knowledge, not perfection. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice. If money worries ever make you anxious or upset, talk to a parent, teacher or counsellor.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Many professional investors say the hardest part is not analysis but managing themselves, and a journal is one of their favourite tools.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MIND CHECKLIST
1. Feeling: what am I feeling right now, such as fear, excitement, boredom or FOMO?
2. Source: where did this idea come from, and do they gain if I act?
3. Facts: what facts do I have, and what is only a story?
4. Opposite view: what is the best argument against this?
5. Anchor: would I buy at today's price if I owned nothing?
6. Plan: are my size, stop and target written down?
7. Wait: have I waited at least 24 hours?
8. Record: have I logged it in my journal?

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE JOURNAL
Add a feeling column to your trade journal. After each trade, note the date, the idea, the reason, the result and what you felt. Once a month, compare impulsive trades with planned trades. The numbers show your own habits.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON TRAPS
• Skipping the checklist when you feel sure.
• Journaling only the wins.
• Trading to win back a loss.
• Changing rules in the middle of a trade.

🍕 MINI CASE: WHAT THE JOURNAL SHOWED
Meera takes 20 practice trades in her simulator. She labels 8 of them as FOMO or impulse trades and wins 2, a win rate of 2 ÷ 8 x 100 = 25%. Her 12 planned trades win 7, a win rate of 7 ÷ 12 x 100 = 58.3%. Overall she wins 9 of 20, which is 45%. The journal shows that her impulse trades were the weak spot. She adds a rule: no trade without the checklist.

🧪 TRY IT: BUILD YOUR OWN
In a fictional journal, 10 trades are logged: 4 impulsive with 1 win and 6 planned with 4 wins. Work out the win rate of each group. Then fill in the eight checklist lines for an idea you have and discuss them with a parent, teacher or guardian.
(Answer: impulsive: 1 ÷ 4 x 100 = 25%. Planned: 4 ÷ 6 x 100 = 66.7%. A feeling column helps you see which habits help and which hurt.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A checklist slows you down and a journal keeps you honest. Know your biases, use rules, and practise on a simulator. No method guarantees profit, and a parent or guardian should be part of any real money decision.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the mind checklist?
options: To slow you down and check your feelings, sources and plan before acting
quiz.explanation: The checklist adds a pause and a structure to decisions.

quiz.question: 2 wins out of 8 impulsive trades is what win rate?
Why add a feeling column to your journal?
options: To see which emotions lead to your best and worst trades
quiz.explanation: Linking feelings to results shows your patterns.

quiz.question: Which source of a trading idea deserves extra caution?
options: Someone who gains if you act
quiz.explanation: People who benefit from your action may be biased.

quiz.question: Does any checklist guarantee profits?
options: No, risk always remains, so practise on a simulator and involve a parent or guardian
quiz.explanation: No method removes risk.
